background.text: Well, Fareed, I think it's important to answer that question on two levels. On one level, we have to take ourselves back to February of 2022. And the world, all of the experts, all of the world predicted that Russia, when it mobilized and launched its brutal invasion of Ukraine, would take the capital city of Kyiv in a week, that Ukraine would fall, that the Russians would subjugate Ukraine rapidly. And the Ukrainian people stood up and basically stopped that from happening. And today, Kyiv is where you're sitting as a free and independent city, and Ukraine is a free and independent country. So at a macro level, Putin's main objective in this war, which was basically to wipe Ukraine off the map, has failed. But we have to answer it at a critical second level, which is today, not February of 2022, but September of 2024. And there are challenges in terms of holding the line in the east. There are challenges in terms of the vicious aerial attacks that are crashing down on cities, including one of the deadliest and most destructive attacks on civilian infrastructure at the end of August. There are so many other deprivations and hardships being visited upon the Ukrainian people that it remains incumbent on those of us in the West. And I think we need to continue to work with the United States to continue to push with urgency to get Ukraine the tools that it needs to defend itself and to be able to push back against this aggression, which continues even as Ukraine inflicts massive daily casualties on the Russian forces.

background.text: Well, again, to answer this question, I have to take us back to April of this year, just before the supplemental pass, the United States funding package for Ukraine. In the months that followed, the Ukrainian defenses have become more stout in many critical places. And Ukraine has taken bold and assertive steps as well in the war, pushing forward. I meet with my team every single day to think about what are the implements, the tools we need to put into place to help stabilize that front and make sure that those grinding advances by the Russians are met with stiff resistance and also that we deny Russia the capacity to really have any kind of breakthrough that would lead to them gaining strategically from their continued push in the east.

have imposed there are logistical challenges there are challenges associated with the defense industrial base and the actual production of munitions we are literally taking 155 shells off the line ukraine that was not an easy thing to do it required us to get our allies and partners to come along frankly it required our bureaucracy to come along but it's that kind of thing that we have to do Sullivan was also a senior advisor to the U.S. government for the Iran nuclear negotiations and a visiting professor at Yale Law School.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: So talk a little bit more about these air defenses, because as you know, the problem of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure, particularly energy infrastructure, is really crippling Ukrainian society. You have power outages now that are as long as eight, nine hours. It means work becomes very difficult. It means obviously schools, hospitals, all of that. Life grinds to a halt. People are leaving as a result. Is there any way to secure Ukraine's energy infrastructure in the short term?

ground_truth: I think there are three elements to this. And again, this is something I meet on with my team every single day. The first element is additional air defense systems. We announced five at NATO, five strategic systems, four Patriots and a SAMP-T. We still have to get one of our partners to conclude the delivery on that. We have to get additional systems, and we are in the process right now of securing those from partners for delivery to Ukraine. So that's one. The second element is more what we call passive protection. Many of these energy transformers or substations or other elements of the energy infrastructure are being hit not by ballistic missiles, but by Iranian drones. The damage from those drones can be abated considerably by building up the kinds of concrete barriers that are necessary essentially to neutralize them. That takes the pressure off the air defense system. Ukraine has done a lot of work on that. It's done a lot of work on the air defense system. It's done a lot of work on the air defense system. It's done a lot of work on the air defense system. It's done a lot of work on pretty well on this, but frankly, there's more to be done. And we're trying to deliver the tools to be able for them to build that out around more energy infrastructure. And then the third is rapid repair. The United States has put hundreds of millions of dollars just this week into efforts to rapidly repair energy so that we keep the gigawatts online, stabilize the grid, and keep it going towards winter. But this is the kind of thing that's an all-hands-on-deck, everyday effort, because of the relentlessness and the severity with which Russia is trying to hit the energy grid and plunge Ukraine into cold and dark, especially as winter approaches.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: In a separate conversation with me, that will air on my program on Sunday, President Zelensky was relentless on the issue of letting Ukraine strike back into Russia at the launching pads, the airplanes and their bases, wherever the missile, the drone, the plane originated from, allowing Ukraine to strike at those targets inside Russia. His worry is that by the time you will approve that kind of strike, you'll say you can do it for 200 meters, but the Russians will have pulled back 500 to 500, sorry, kilometers. The Russians will pull back to 500 kilometers. In other words, they'll always be one step ahead of the Western permissions and therefore escape any real damage. What would you say to him?

ground_truth: Well, first, just to level set, President Biden, when the Russians launched another brutal assault across the frontier into Kharkiv, President Biden authorized strike across the border using U.S. munitions, basically on the proposition that if you're coming across the border, the Ukrainians have to, on a common sense and moral basis, be able to hit back. The only system that the U.S. has, to this point, not authorized for use across the Russian border is the Atakom system. It has a total range of 300 kilometers. So I'm not sure that system really implicates the concern you've just laid out of moving back to 400 or 500 kilometers, because as a practical matter, it cannot hit targets at 400 or 500 kilometers. That's not me revealing some secret. That's a yesterday, as you all know, with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. It's part of the reason I couldn't be there in person today, was that was an important meeting, a strategy session on Ukraine in preparation for President Zelensky coming to meet with the president in New York the week after next at the General Assembly. They obviously discussed this issue. It's been much talked about in the press. I think it's important for me to say I don't have an announcement today on this issue. This is something the president, the prime minister discussed, and I will leave it at that for now. I understand Ukraine's perspective on it. But, you know, rather than me trying to elaborate reasoning one way or the other, this is something that I think is the subject of intense consultation among allies and partners and will be between the president and President Zelensky.
